analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: A full repeal of the estate and gift taxes drew 204 House cosponsors but never left the Ways and Means Committee and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax completely, effective immediately upon enactment. In the late 1990s, the estate tax applied only to estates above a large exemption — roughly $650,000 per person, with special treatment for some farms and small businesses — so repeal would chiefly spare heirs of the very largest estates. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and saw no further action before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates. In the late 1990s most family estates fell below the tax-free exemption and owed nothing; the families that owed the tax were those with multi-million-dollar estates, and repeal would eliminate tax rates the bill's own findings put between 37% and 55% at the margin [S3]. Owners of large family businesses and farms would also gain, as they sometimes had to sell assets to pay the tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code — the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes — for estates of people dying and gifts made after enactment [S2][S3].

The bill's own findings state the taxes took between 37% and 55% of after-tax savings at the margin and produced about 1% of federal revenue in fiscal 1998, meaning repeal would deliver large sums to a narrow group while costing the Treasury a comparatively small share of revenue [S3].

Sponsors argued repeal would spare family businesses from liquidating assets to pay the tax and cited a Joint Economic Committee study claiming the taxes had reduced the U.S. capital stock by $497 billion [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury, and therefore taxpayers generally. The bill's own findings concede these taxes raised about 1% of total federal revenue in fiscal year 1998 — real money that would have to be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or smaller spending [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax fell almost entirely on very large estates: with the late-1990s exemption around $650,000 per person (higher for qualifying farms and small businesses), ordinary families' estates already passed largely tax-free, so the repeal's benefits would concentrate on the wealthiest households [S3].

Repeal eliminates roughly 1% of federal revenue by the bill's own accounting, which would need to be replaced through other taxes or deficits — costs spread across all taxpayers while the savings go to a few thousand very large estates each year [S3].

The bill's claims that the taxes cut the capital stock by $497 billion and boost GDP on repeal are findings supplied by the sponsors and their cited study, not established facts; the revenue and distribution effects were the core of the debate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the families who actually owed the estate tax, repeal is a large, direct windfall. For everyone else, the bill offers little: most estates owed nothing in the late 1990s, and the revenue loss — about 1% of federal receipts by the bill's own figures — would be borne broadly. The bill's strongest argument is about farms and small businesses, but those filers already had special valuation and deferral rules, which blunts the claim that repeal was needed to save them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced in January 1999 and the committee never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Cox introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, the opening day of the 106th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
The bill drew 204 cosponsors — 193 Republicans and 11 Democrats [S4].
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral; the Congress ended January 3, 2001 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S. Treasury kept roughly 1% of federal revenue that repeal would have eliminated, spread across all taxpayers, while heirs of very large estates remained subject to the tax. Sponsors' own numbers put the annual revenue at stake in the tens of billions.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Cox
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Family Heritage Preservation Act on January 6, 1999 and recruited cosponsors

for.name: 204 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (193 Republicans, 11 Democrats), including House Majority Leader Dick Armey and Majority Whip Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill more cosponsors than the 218 needed to pass the House if all had voted for it

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving it to die in committee

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Opposed full estate tax repeal; vetoed a similar Republican estate-tax repeal bill in 2000

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 204 cosponsors, 193 were Republicans and 11 were Democrats — broad Republican backing with a small bipartisan tail [S4].

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: Repeal would eliminate marginal taxes of 37% to 55% on estates above the late-1990s exemption — a benefit flowing to a small group of very large estates. The cost of replacing that revenue, about 1% of federal receipts by the bill's own figures, falls on taxpayers broadly.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and trust services
industries.note: The bill's own findings describe families spending billions annually on accountants and lawyers to structure trusts that avoid the tax; repeal would eliminate much of that work.
Sponsors argued estate taxes force some business owners to sell assets to pay the tax, though qualifying farms and businesses already had special valuation and deferral rules in the late-1990s code.
